clue.text: Refusal implied with it?

parts.note: surface reading: a no hinted at alongside something
setter's reading: the phrase itself describes the word NO turned round, which reads as the second word of the answer

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a refusal is being hinted at.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: switch the letters of NO and you get ON, so 'switched on' implies a refusal. The phrase also means fashionable or alert, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone alert and trendy is described in idiom as both switched on and with it.

clue.text: Squat painter's second son's given up for year

indicators.note: one thing given up in exchange for another is swapped out and replaced

parts.note: George Stubbs, the English painter famous for horses
S is the abbreviation for son; it is the second S in the painter's name that goes
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A painter's younger son has abandoned his chosen career after a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second son' does not mean a younger child: it points at the second letter S in STUBBS, which Y replaces.
explanation.definitionFit: Squat and stubby are both adjectives for something short and thick.

clue.text: Off limits West African peninsula

indicators.note: Off says the letter that follows comes away from the country's name

parts.note: Liberia is a West African country
the opening letter of limits

explanation.surface: A West African region has been declared off limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off limits' looks like one phrase meaning forbidden, but it splits: L, the first of limits, comes off LIBERIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iberian peninsula holds Spain and Portugal in south-western Europe.

clue.text: Smart Scots know current colour: yellow

parts.note: smart in dress means chic
ken is the Scots verb to know
a live wire carries current
red is a colour

explanation.surface: A list of things a smart Scot knows about a colour, ending on yellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellow' looks like one more colour in the list; here it means cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is slang for cowardly, and a coward is called chicken-livered.

clue.text: One possibly pots plant with a second hidden feature

indicators.note: to pot a plant is to set it inside a container, so one word holds another

parts.note: e.g., for example, introduces one possibility
the aster is a daisy-like garden flower
a second copy of the same abbreviation for example

explanation.surface: Someone pots up a plant and gives it a second, concealed feature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pots plant' reads as gardening; it is a container instruction, and the first abbreviation holds both the flower and its twin.
explanation.definitionFit: Software and film makers call a concealed joke or bonus an Easter egg, after the chocolate treats children hunt for.

clue.text: Olivier's principal role that's moving to the observer?

indicators.note: the principal part of a name is its leading letter

parts.note: the opening letter of Olivier
an actor's role is a part

explanation.surface: A theatre fan describes Laurence Olivier's leading role as moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' looks like emotional praise for Olivier; the definition means art that appears to move before the viewer's eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art uses optical patterns that seem to shimmer and shift when looked at.

clue.text: Owner of shiny hooter ready for people in Hanoi

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Edward Lear's creature with a luminous nose
second meaning: the currency of Vietnam, ready being slang for cash

explanation.surface: Someone with a glowing nose is prepared for the people of Hanoi.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's nonsense poem is 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose'; hooter is slang for nose, and ready (or readies) is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear named his glowing-nosed creature the Dong, and the same word is Vietnam's monetary unit.

clue.text: Passing exchange by inside half

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the passing move

parts.note: a one-two is a quick give-and-go pass in football
by day means in the day

explanation.surface: A football commentator describes a quick passing move with an inside half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside half' sounds like a football position, but half is the definition and inside is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A half is a proportion of fifty per cent, the same as one out of every two.

clue.text: I can't see in mirror very well and it's caught by stray leg

indicators.note: a mirror shows things back to front
something caught is held inside whatever caught it
letters that stray wander out of their places

parts.note: it in the sense of sex appeal is abbreviated SA
taken as written
very well, as an agreement, means yes

explanation.surface: Someone complains of poor vision in the mirror and of a leg that wanders.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is written in the first person, as if the false eye were speaking. The 's of it's stands for is, joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An artificial eye made of glass gives its wearer no sight, so it could truthfully say it cannot see.

clue.text: Serial overnighter you'll upset, along with the others

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and its order thrown into disarray

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps staying the night will annoy you and everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: A backpacker who stays at hostels night after night is a habitual overnight guest.

clue.text: Leaving service, retiring one gives back baby carriers

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing, going back the way it came
what is leaving departs from the word, taking its letters away

parts.note: to give back is to return
the Royal Navy, a branch of the armed services
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A man leaving the armed forces finds that retirement brings back a pram.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is read out of order, and 'service' is not a church or tennis term but one of the armed forces, the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: The womb carries an unborn child, so plural wombs are carriers of babies.

clue.text: Serial drama very good each time

parts.note: 'very good' as a reply of acceptance can be said as 'so be it'; so also means very
a pop means each, as in a pound a pop
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A television serial is very good every time it airs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pop' is informal for each, as in 'ten pounds a pop'.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running broadcast series about the lives of ordinary characters, originally sponsored by detergent makers.

clue.text: Builder that's disgusting getting stuck into cheese

indicators.note: something stuck into another thing ends up inside it

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese
ick is an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: A workman tucks greedily into some foul cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: A brickie is British slang for a bricklayer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bricklayer is a construction worker, the informal word being a familiar term on British building sites.

clue.text: Acute condition, back fatty tissue restricting function

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so one word surrounds another
back says the following word runs the other way

parts.note: suet is hard fat from around the kidneys
tan is the tangent function in trigonometry

explanation.surface: A doctor notes an acute back condition where fatty tissue restricts movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' seems to be the sore part of the body; it reverses the fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Lockjaw is a serious bacterial infection with sudden severe muscle spasms, an acute illness.

clue.text: Swan's mate? Where there's a Will …

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the wife of the Swan of Avon, Shakespeare's nickname
second meaning: the proverb ends 'there's a way', which in Shakespearean English is 'hath a way'

explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson called Shakespeare the Sweet Swan of Avon, and his wife was Will's partner. Her surname sounds like the old form of the proverb's ending, 'hath a way'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's wife married him in 1582, making her the Bard's spouse and the woman beside Will.

clue.text: What centaurs and minotaurs are doing around flat

indicators.note: around puts one word on both sides of the other

parts.note: at means doing, as in 'what are you at?'
both creatures are partly human, so they are part men

explanation.surface: A question about what mythical half-human beasts get up to.
explanation.walkthrough: A centaur is half horse and a minotaur half bull. 'Flat' could be an adjective, but it is the British word for a set of rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat is the British word for a set of rooms on one floor, which Americans call an apartment.

clue.text: Hacker cunningly blocked by fresh market research data backup

indicators.note: fresh means new, so what is left is made into something new
what is blocked is stopped from getting through, so those letters never reach the answer
cunningly warns that the letters to be stopped are not sitting together in order but are scattered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; these six letters are the ones removed

explanation.surface: A cunning hacker is foiled by new market research, and the data is backed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word before the definition is wordplay: 'Hacker' is not a computer criminal to find a synonym for, but six letters to strike out of the long phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A tape streamer is a drive that copies a computer's data onto magnetic tape for safekeeping.

clue.text: Wherever you are in the US capital new and exciting play is screened

definitions.text: Wherever you are in the US

indicators.note: what is screened is hidden behind or inside something else

parts.note: capital and ace are both old-fashioned words for excellent

indicators.note: exciting stirs things up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wherever you are in America's capital, a new and exciting play is being shown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' seems to be Washington; it means first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: American English uses this compound adverb where Britons say anywhere, meaning in whatever location.

clue.text: Sadly no state will receive energetic spiritual leader

indicators.note: receiving something means taking it in
sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken as written
zingy means lively and energetic

explanation.surface: A lament that no nation will welcome a vigorous religious figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits his real exile: the Dalai Lama has no state of his own.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the personal name of the fourteenth Dalai Lama, Tibetan Buddhism's exiled religious head.

clue.text: Grain as nourishing heart of tiny duck

indicators.note: nourishing something means taking it in, so the word holds others

parts.note: qua is Latin for as, in the capacity of

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle

parts.note: the middle two letters of tiny
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O

explanation.surface: Grain feeds a little duckling at its heart.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of zero, hence O.
explanation.definitionFit: Quinoa is the seed of an Andean plant, eaten and cooked like a cereal crop.

clue.text: Bloodhound on the trail of egotist's favourite plant

indicators.note: a hound on the trail follows behind, so this piece comes after the other

parts.note: an egotist's favourite person is me
a bloodhound is slang for a detective, as is dick

explanation.surface: A tracking dog follows the scent of a vain man's favourite plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloodhound' suggests a dog, but it is slang for a detective, as is dick.
explanation.definitionFit: Medick is a clover-like plant of the pea family, including lucerne.

clue.text: Special messenger retired from Fleet Street?

parts.note: ex means former, retired
Fleet Street in London was home to the national newspapers, so it stands for the press

explanation.surface: A dispatch rider who once worked for the London newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Express itself left Fleet Street, the old home of British newspapers, which makes the question mark apt.
explanation.definitionFit: An express is a messenger sent specially with urgent news, an older sense of the word.

clue.text: After evacuating civilians, climbing ladder

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: à la means after the manner of

indicators.note: evacuating a word empties out its inside, leaving only the ends

parts.note: the first and last letters of civilians

explanation.surface: Once the civilians are cleared out, a soldier goes up a ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: Scala is Latin for ladder or staircase, as in Milan's La Scala opera house.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for a ladder or flight of steps is used in English for anatomical and architectural ladder-like structures.

clue.text: Underground TV

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a pirate broadcaster; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Londoners call their metro railway by this nickname, and older slang uses the same phrase for the television set, after its cathode-ray tube.

clue.text: Joe storms after Mike

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to storm is both to rave and to rage, so the two verbs side by side

explanation.surface: Joe flies into a temper after Mike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' just puts M first. Joe looks like a name; here it is the ordinary person.
explanation.definitionFit: An average Joe is a typical, unremarkable person, as is the everyman figure of the answer.

clue.text: Indians wear this uniform, acquired for nothing in Long Island

indicators.note: a thing acquired for another is taken in exchange, so one letter swaps for another

parts.note: Long plus I for island
O looks like zero
Uniform is U in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Indians wear a uniform that they got free on Long Island.
explanation.walkthrough: The U is exchanged for the O of LONG I.
explanation.definitionFit: A lungi is a cloth wrapped around the waist like a sarong, traditional dress in South Asia.

clue.text: Unimpeded, move along fine ridge

indicators.note: this phrase says the abbreviation for a fine pencil lead travels along the word to the far end

parts.note: unimpeded means free

explanation.surface: Someone told to move along freely, with a fine ridge in view.
explanation.walkthrough: The F of FREE moves from the front to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A reef is a ridge of rock or coral lying at or near the sea's surface.

clue.text: Rabbit rating amphibian

parts.note: to rabbit, in British slang, is to chatter, as is natter
a rating is an ordinary sailor, as is a jack tar

explanation.surface: A rabbit assessing a frog or toad.
explanation.walkthrough: Rabbit (on) is British for chatter, from rhyming slang 'rabbit and pork' for talk; a rating is a non-officer in the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: The natterjack is a European toad with a yellow stripe down its back.
